<reason>Both sides built coherent, well-structured cases, but B's incentive-mechanism argument proved more resilient under pressure. B's sharpest move was turning A's own claim that "a refusal itself becomes verified information neighbors can act on" [A2.4] into a liability: a bright-line rule collapses honest hesitation and deliberate concealment into the same signal, which rationally pushes states toward earlier, harder denial. A's Rebuttal 2 answered this at the moment of outbreak ("denial starts a clock"), but never squarely addressed B's escalated point in Rebuttal 2 that governments would pre-organize surveillance gaps and reporting channels *before* any outbreak, precisely because the rule's existence is known in advance — a claim B crystallized cleanly in its closing ("what does a government do the moment it learns this rule exists?"). A's closing restated the "confirmation gap, not the outbreak, is what's hidden" line rather than engaging that anticipatory-concealment framing or B's related critique that a host-veto-free confirmation right could turn an overwhelmed ministry's provisional uncertainty into a premature public "headline," undermining A's own claim that verification is straightforward relief. B's alternative (capacity-building, no-stigma incentives) was consistently positioned as avoiding the very reflex B argued the coercive regime creates, giving B a cleaner throughline across rounds. A's insurance framing and reputational-enforcement rebuttal were solid and rhetorically polished, but by the final exchange B had identified and sustained pressure on the load-bearing tension in A's model that A did not fully neutralize.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Rebuttal 1 turning [A2.4] ("a refusal itself becomes verified information") back on A, reframed and extended into the anticipatory-concealment argument in B's Rebuttal 2 and Closing, which A's Closing did not directly rebut.</best_rebuttal>
